question: For initially solid iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles examined across the premelting and melting regime, limited understanding of their thermal response constrains interpretation of application limits and high-temperature synthesis, where cooling must consolidate the solid solution. Prior studies of Ag, Au, Al, and Pd nanoparticles established that nanoscale phase-transition behavior can differ markedly among particle systems, but findings from single-metal particles do not resolve the response of chemically complex nanoparticles. Work on bimetallic particles further demonstrated that chemical complexity can produce varied configurations, while research on high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles remains sparse and has not established the governing physics for this composition. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its premelting and melting behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline particle, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, prior findings that support it, and an observation that would decisively falsify it.
